cards.title: Ionic strength: compare charge first, then ion size
cards.difficulty_signal: May 2025 examiners called a radius-and-bond-strength question very challenging (25M.1A.SL.TZ1.10). An older lattice enthalpy question had a Difficulty Index of 43% (09N.1.HL.TZ0.17).

evidence.note: Answer A: the pair with the two smaller ions has the strongest attraction.
Most chose the same wrong option; the link between radius and bond strength is not well understood.
Many thought the larger potassium ion gave a more endothermic lattice enthalpy than the smaller sodium ion.
Top distractor when ordering ionic radii put the anions before the cations.
Na⁺ and O²⁻ radius comparison: one mark for isoelectronic, one for more protons in Na⁺.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: lattice enthalpy measures ionic bond strength, influenced by ion radius and charge.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show tables of values. Exams give only element names, so you must infer ions, charges and sizes.

trap_boundaries: Reported misconception: a larger cation gives a more endothermic lattice enthalpy (09N.1.HL.TZ0.17).
Comparing an ion with its own atom does not answer a comparison of two ions (18N.2.SL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial thinking picks one small ion. The full answer needs both ions smallest once the charges tie.

disguises: Elements named instead of ions
'Strongest attraction' standing in for greatest lattice enthalpy
Ranking a mixed list of cations and anions by radius
3_novel_application.heuristic: Convert names to ions, compare charges, and only then compare sizes.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: one mark, all or nothing. A written radius comparison gave separate marks for isoelectronic and for more protons (18N.2.SL.TZ0.4).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip electron configurations and any attempt to calculate the attraction.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 10 prints ionic radii with charges. Section 16 shows LiCl 864, NaCl 790, KCl 720 kJ mol⁻¹: smaller cation, larger lattice enthalpy.

rules: If charges tie, an option with two larger ions cannot be strongest.
Higher charges usually outrank smaller ions: BaO 3054 exceeds LiF 1049 in section 16. Check the booklet when both factors differ.

walkthrough.question:
Each pair of elements below forms an ionic compound. Which pair gives the compound with the greatest attraction between its ions?
A. Li and O
B. Li and Se
C. K and O
D. K and Se
walkthrough.key_idea: Charges are equal in every option, so the smallest ions attract most.
walkthrough.question_type: Rank ionic bond or lattice strength
walkthrough.careful: Compare charge first; radius decides only when charges tie.
procedure: Write the charge of each element's ion.
Compare the charges across the options.
If charges tie, compare the ionic radii.
Choose higher charges, then smaller ions.
tricks: Down a group, ions of equal charge get bigger; across periods, read section 10.
Check the trend in section 16: LiCl 864 exceeds KCl 720.
if_lost: What charge does each metal's ion carry?
Do the options differ in their ion charges?
If charges match, what else changes the attraction?
How does ion size change going down a group?

1_context.short: Tests lattice strength from ion charge and ion size.
1_context.why: The syllabus names radius and charge as the two factors, so swapping ions tests whether you apply them in order.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from metal reactivity; the question is about the attraction between the ions.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: lattice enthalpy measures ionic bond strength, influenced by ion radius and charge.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books compare listed lattice enthalpies. Here only element names appear, so you must deduce the ions first.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only the pair with both ions smallest earns the mark.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Attraction grows as opposite charges get closer, so the smaller pair wins when the charges are equal.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Thinking a larger ion gives a stronger lattice, a reported error (09N.1.HL.TZ0.17).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: One small ion paired with one large ion is not enough; the mark needs both small.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B and C each have one small ion. A has two, so its ions sit closest.

3_novel_application.short: Elements are named, so deduce the ions before comparing.
3_novel_application.why: Nothing in the stem mentions radius or charge. Writing the ions exposes the usual charge-and-size comparison.
3_novel_application.avoid: Comparing atoms instead of the ions they form.
3_novel_application.disguise: No radii, charges or lattice enthalpies appear; 'attraction' replaces the phrase lattice enthalpy.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Turn every name into an ion, then ask which pair sits closest.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: one mark, with no credit for working.
4_command_terms.why: Only the letter scores, so a quick ranking is enough and exact values add nothing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Looking up every radius when the group trend already decides.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the pair with the greatest electrostatic attraction between its ions.

5_time_efficiency.short: Charges, then sizes: about twenty seconds in total.
5_time_efficiency.why: Once the charges tie, two group comparisons settle it: one for the metals and one for the non-metals.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing full electron configurations for all four elements.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip configurations and any calculation of attraction.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 10 lists ionic radii with their charges.
6_data_booklet.why: Reading radii replaces memorising sizes, and section 16 confirms that a smaller ion gives a larger lattice enthalpy.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading atomic radius by mistake: Li is 130 as an atom but 76 as an ion.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 10 shows Li 76 (1+) and O 140 (2−). Section 16 shows LiCl 864 and KCl 720.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Nothing beyond the group trend; radii and charges are printed.

7_elimination.short: Any option using a larger ion loses to its smaller swap.
7_elimination.why: With equal charges, replacing an ion by a smaller one in its group always strengthens attraction, so three options fall without numbers.
7_elimination.avoid: Stopping after ruling out D; B and C can also go.

definitely_wrong.rule: Both ions are the larger of their group pair, so it is the weakest.
Swapping Se for the smaller O, same charge, gives stronger attraction.
Swapping K for the smaller Li, same charge, gives stronger attraction.

walkthrough.answer: A. All options combine a 1+ ion with a 2− ion, so size decides. Li⁺ and O²⁻ are the smaller ions, so they attract most strongly.

cards.title: Moles of an ion: read the formula, and check ions exist
cards.difficulty_signal: The related chloride-ion question was among the hardest: 26.81% correct at HL and 28.15% at SL (15M.1.HL.TZ1.3, 15M.1.SL.TZ1.4). Over 70% managed the phosphate version (24N.1.HL.TZ0.1).

evidence.note: Answer C: moles of compound multiplied by two phosphates per formula.
Over 70% could find the amount of phosphate ions in a mass of calcium phosphate.
Only 26.81% correct; most picked a molecular compound, which contains no chloride ions.
Only 28.15% correct; students had to judge ionic versus molecular as well as the quantity.
Most common mistake concerned the two sulfates present, giving 4.0 instead of 2.0.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.2: deduce formulas of ionic compounds, including polyatomic ions. S2.1.3: ionic compounds are represented by empirical formulas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach moles of a compound. Exams ask for moles of one ion inside it, or whether that ion exists at all.

trigger_phrases: moles of compound × ions per formula unit
molecular compound contains no such ions
trap_boundaries: Stopping at moles of compound gives a listed wrong option (24N.1.HL.TZ0.1).
A molecular chloride contains no chloride ions, so it cannot be counted (15M.1.HL.TZ1.3).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial thinking finds moles of compound. The full answer also applies the ion count and checks the bonding type.

disguises: A stoichiometry question that is really about formula reading
A list of chlorides where one is molecular
Polyatomic ion in brackets with a subscript
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask: is it ionic, and how many of this exact ion are in one formula unit?

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing. Working earns nothing, and each wrong step usually matches a distractor.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip finding Mr yourself when given; skip percentage composition routes.

6_data_booklet.hack: No booklet table helps here. Polyatomic ion formulas such as phosphate and sulfate are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Mass below Mr means under one mole of compound, so cap the ion answer at the subscript.
The answer for ions must differ from moles of compound unless the count is one.

walkthrough.question:
A sample of calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂ (Mr = 310.18), has a mass of 103.39 g. What amount, in mol, of phosphate ions, PO₄³⁻, does it contain?
A. 0.11
B. 0.33
C. 0.67
D. 2.00
walkthrough.key_idea: One formula unit holds two phosphate ions, so double the compound's moles.
walkthrough.question_type: Moles of ions from a formula
walkthrough.careful: Multiply by the ion count after finding moles of compound.
procedure: Check the compound is ionic, so the ion exists.
Find moles of compound: mass divided by Mr.
Count that ion in one formula unit.
Multiply moles of compound by that count.
tricks: A subscript outside brackets multiplies everything inside, so count the bracket.
Spot simple fractions: compare the mass with Mr before reaching for a calculator.
if_lost: What does the subscript outside the bracket tell you?
How many moles of the whole compound do you have?
How many phosphate ions are in one formula unit?

1_context.short: Tests reading ion counts from an ionic formula.
1_context.why: An empirical formula gives the ratio of ions in the lattice, so its subscripts convert moles of compound into moles of ion.
1_context.avoid: Treating the Mr as the mass of a phosphate ion.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: ionic compounds exist as lattices represented by empirical formulas.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise moles of a compound. This question asks for moles of one ion inside it.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The mark needs moles of compound multiplied by two.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Each formula unit contains two phosphates, so ion moles are double the compound moles.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Miscounting the polyatomic ions; two sulfates caused the commonest error in 09N.1.SL.TZ0.5.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: 0.33 is the compound's moles, not phosphate's, so stopping there scores nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B stops at moles of compound. C multiplies by the two phosphates in each formula.

3_novel_application.short: Looks like plain moles; really a formula-reading question.
3_novel_application.why: The calculation is easy once you see the stem asks about an ion, not the whole compound.
3_novel_application.avoid: Answering for the compound because the Mr given is the compound's.
3_novel_application.disguise: A mass and Mr suggest one division, but the requested species is one ion.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Underline what is counted, then ask how many are in one formula.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: one mark, with no credit for working.
4_command_terms.why: Each slip lands on a printed distractor, so the checking must be done before choosing.
4_command_terms.avoid: Choosing the first printed number that matches an intermediate step.
4_command_terms.demands: Give the amount of phosphate ions, not of calcium phosphate.

5_time_efficiency.short: Two moves: divide, then multiply by the ion count.
5_time_efficiency.why: The mass is close to a simple fraction of the Mr, so little calculation is needed.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Recalculating the Mr; it is already given.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip recalculating Mr and working out calcium's amount.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet table is needed; everything is in the stem.
6_data_booklet.why: Formula, mass and Mr are all given, so only the meaning of brackets and subscripts has to come from you.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Searching the booklet for phosphate; polyatomic ions are not listed there.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None needed: the formula itself is the table to read.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Phosphate is PO₄³⁻, and a subscript after brackets multiplies the whole ion. Neither is in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Compare with one-third of a mole of compound by eye.
7_elimination.why: 103 is about a third of 310, and two phosphates per unit must raise the ion amount above that.
7_elimination.avoid: Choosing 2.00 because it matches the subscript.

definitely_wrong.rule: Under one mole of compound cannot hold two moles of phosphate.
Equals the compound's moles, so it ignores the two phosphates.
Below the compound's moles, yet each unit has more than one phosphate.

walkthrough.answer: C. 103.39 ÷ 310.18 = 0.333 mol of Ca₃(PO₄)₂. Each formula unit has 2 phosphates, so 0.333 × 2 = 0.67 mol.

cards.title: Structure from data: use melting point and conductivity together
cards.difficulty_signal: Conductivity by ions rather than electrons is flagged repeatedly (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6, 15M.2.SL.TZ2.3). Only 40% stated a correct physical property in 18N.2.SL.TZ0.4.

evidence.note: Answer B: high melting point with poor solid and good molten conductivity.
Slightly more students could identify an ionic solid from its physical properties.
Top distractor suggests students used conductivity data but ignored melting point.
73% correct; those choosing the next option should have considered conductivity more carefully.
Many spoke of delocalised electrons rather than ions moving when molten.
Far too many linked conductivity in molten compounds with mobile electrons.
Accepted properties: brittle, high melting point, low volatility, conducts when molten, not as a solid.
Most named ionic bonding, but very few explained why the lattice is brittle.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: explain physical properties of ionic compounds, including volatility, electrical conductivity and solubility.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books list properties per structure. Exams give raw data and expect every reading to be matched to particles.

trigger_phrases: ions in fixed positions in the solid
trap_boundaries: Mobile electrons in a molten ionic compound is a repeatedly reported error (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6, 15M.2.SL.TZ2.3).
A chemical property, or a property of a metal, was a reported mistake when a physical property was asked for (18N.2.SL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial answers state the property. Full answers name the charge carrier, which is ions, and link it to the state.

disguises: Unnamed substance in a data table
Unfamiliar compound such as a lanthanum halide asked about brittleness
Molten aluminium, where electrons are the carrier
3_novel_application.heuristic: For each reading, ask which particles could move in that state.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: all or nothing. Written property answers give one mark per valid point (18N.2.SL.TZ0.4), with no reason needed for State.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip naming example compounds; the data alone decides.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 16 lattice enthalpies, such as NaCl 790 and MgO 3791 kJ mol⁻¹, show why ionic melting points are high. Melting points themselves are not in the section text provided.

rules: Good solid conductivity rules out ionic; it points to metallic, except graphite, a covalent network.
A high melting point rules out simple molecular.
Conduction only when molten rules out covalent network.

walkthrough.question:
A substance melts at 714 °C. It conducts electricity poorly as a solid but well when molten. Which structure is it most likely to have?
A. Simple molecular
B. Ionic lattice
C. Covalent network
D. Metallic lattice
walkthrough.key_idea: Conducting only when molten, with a high melting point, means ions freed on melting.
walkthrough.careful: Use melting point and conductivity together, not conductivity alone.
procedure: Read the conductivity as a solid, then when molten.
Ask which particles can carry charge in each state.
Use melting point to separate weak from strong forces.
Choose the structure that fits every reading.
tricks: Good solid conductor suggests a metal; fails for graphite, a covalent network.
Poor solid, good molten is the pattern to recognise; check both columns.
if_lost: What must be able to move for electricity to flow?
Which particles are free in the molten state but fixed in the solid?
Does the melting point suggest weak or strong forces?

1_context.short: Tests matching raw data to a type of structure.
1_context.why: Each structure has its own charge carriers and forces, so a few readings are enough to identify it.
1_context.avoid: Matching only one reading, then choosing straight away.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: explain physical properties of ionic compounds, including electrical conductivity and volatility.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books describe known compounds' properties. This gives unnamed data and asks you to work backwards to structure.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only one structure fits all three readings.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Ions are locked in the solid and free when molten, and strong attraction explains the high melting point.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Using conductivity but ignoring melting point, as examiners reported in 17M.1.HL.TZ1.9.
trigger_phrases: poor as solid, good when molten
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: An option fitting only one or two readings earns nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: D fails poor solid conduction. A fails 714 °C. C fails molten conduction.

3_novel_application.short: No compound is named; only the data identifies it.
3_novel_application.why: Without a name you cannot rely on metal-plus-non-metal recall, so the particles have to do the reasoning.
3_novel_application.avoid: Thinking mobile electrons carry charge in molten ionic compounds (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6).
3_novel_application.disguise: An unnamed substance with three bare numbers or words replaces a familiar compound.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask what becomes free on melting that was fixed in the solid.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: 'most probable' means best fit to all data.
4_command_terms.why: The wording allows for rare exceptions, so choose the structure fitting everything rather than hunting for special cases.
4_command_terms.avoid: Overthinking unusual substances that the data does not point to.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the structure that best fits all the given properties.

5_time_efficiency.short: Read two conductivities, then confirm with melting point.
5_time_efficiency.why: Conductivity removes most options straight away, and melting point is the final check examiners say students skip.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Recalling example compounds for each option.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip naming example compounds for each option.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 16 supports it, but no lookup is needed.
6_data_booklet.why: Large lattice enthalpies show the strong attraction behind a high melting point, though this question can be answered from the data alone.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Hunting for 714 °C; melting points are not in the section text provided.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Lattice enthalpies such as NaCl 790 and MgO 3791 kJ mol⁻¹ show strong ionic attraction.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Charge carriers per structure are NOT in the booklet: ions, delocalised electrons, or none.

7_elimination.short: Each wrong structure fails a single reading.
7_elimination.why: One mismatch is enough, so each option can go on a single fact, with no calculation at all.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping covalent network just because the melting point is high.

definitely_wrong.rule: Metals conduct well as solids; this solid conducts poorly.
Simple molecular substances melt low and do not conduct when molten.
Covalent networks have no ions to conduct when molten.

walkthrough.answer: B. Ionic lattice: ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten, and strong attraction gives the high melting point.

cards.title: Ionic lattice: name the force and the structure exactly
cards.difficulty_signal: Knowledge of the NaCl structure reached only 52% correct (15N.1.HL.TZ0.9). Written descriptions of ionic bonding are repeatedly flagged as incomplete (19M.2.SL.TZ1.3, 15M.2.HL.TZ2.8, 13M.2.SL.TZ2.5).

evidence.note: Answer D: the lattice breaks apart on dissolving.
Just over 52% correct; candidates are expected to know the sodium chloride structure.
NaCl's cubic lattice must be known; face-centred terms are not required.
Two points: regular lattice of ions, and electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Same two points for Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.
Separate marks: electrostatic attraction, and between oppositely charged ions.
Stating ionic bonding as the nature of the force was wrong; electrostatic attraction was required.
Many called sodium oxide covalent or metallic; others knew it was ionic but described it inadequately.
Only 37% correct on ammonium: bonding inside the ion is electron sharing between atoms.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.2: the ionic bond is electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. S2.1.3: ionic compounds form three-dimensional lattices.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books show a tidy lattice image. Exams test the exact force, the neighbour count, and what happens on dissolving.

trap_boundaries: Naming 'ionic bonding' as the force was not accepted where the nature of the force was asked (13N.2.SL.TZ0.3).
Attraction mentioned without saying between which particles gets only part of the marks (21M.2.SL.TZ1.1).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: One mark for electrostatic attraction alone. Full marks add oppositely charged ions, or a named ion pair, or the lattice point.

disguises: Four true-or-false statements about a figure
An unfamiliar pair such as Fe²⁺ and S²⁻ to describe
A polyatomic ion with covalent bonds inside it
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask which particles are present, what force holds them, and how they are arranged.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Written descriptions give one mark per point, usually two (19M.2.SL.TZ1.3, 21M.2.SL.TZ1.1). MCQ is all or nothing.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip face-centred terms; examiners confirmed they are not required (09M.1.HL.TZ1.10).

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 16 gives NaCl 790 kJ mol⁻¹, showing the attraction is strong. Lattice geometry and neighbour counts are NOT in the booklet.

rules: 'Covalent' between the ions of an ionic lattice is wrong; covalent bonds occur only inside polyatomic ions.
'Weak forces' in an ionic lattice is wrong.
'Molecules of NaCl' is wrong: the formula is empirical.

walkthrough.question:
A figure shows an expanded view of the sodium chloride lattice, built from Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. Which statement about this lattice is true?
A. Covalent bonds hold the ions in place.
B. The attractions within the lattice are very weak.
C. Every sodium ion has four chloride ions around it.
D. The structure breaks apart when it dissolves in water.
walkthrough.key_idea: Strong electrostatic attraction holds the ions; water separates them on dissolving.
walkthrough.question_type: Ionic lattice: true or false statements
walkthrough.careful: NaCl has six neighbours per ion, not four.
procedure: Name the particles and the force in the lattice.
Test each statement against that model.
Check any numbers against the known lattice arrangement.
Choose the only statement that survives.
tricks: 'Covalent' with ionic lattice is false, except for bonds inside polyatomic ions.
In NaCl, each ion has six neighbours of opposite charge.
if_lost: What particles make up this lattice?
What kind of force acts between those particles?
How many opposite ions surround each ion in NaCl?
What happens to the ions when the solid dissolves?

1_context.short: Tests the ionic lattice model through statements.
1_context.why: The ionic bond and lattice arrangement are core knowledge, so each statement checks one part of the model.
1_context.avoid: Relying on the figure to count neighbours; an expanded view can mislead.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.3: ionic compounds exist as three-dimensional lattice structures.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books label a neat lattice. This asks you to reject wrong claims about force and count.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Three statements contradict the model; one survives.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Force type, force strength and neighbour count are all fixed facts, so any statement breaking one of them is false.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Calling ionic forces weak or covalent; examiners reported covalent or metallic answers for Na₂O (19M.2.SL.TZ1.3).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Four neighbours is wrong for NaCl, even though it sounds specific and confident.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A, B and C each misstate force or count. D correctly describes the lattice breaking up.

3_novel_application.short: A figure appears, but the facts alone decide it.
3_novel_application.why: The picture is expanded, so its gaps can suggest weak forces. Your knowledge of the model matters more than appearance.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading the drawn gaps as evidence of weak attraction.
3_novel_application.disguise: A diagram invites counting and visual judgement, when recall of the model is what scores.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Test each statement against particles, force and arrangement, ignoring how the drawing looks.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: exactly one statement is correct.
4_command_terms.why: Only one statement can be right, so finding a clear fault in the others is as useful as proving one.
4_command_terms.avoid: Hunting for hidden faults in a statement that matches the model.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the one statement that agrees with the ionic lattice model.

5_time_efficiency.short: Test each statement once, without studying the figure.
5_time_efficiency.why: Each statement is checked with one fact, so spending time on the figure adds nothing.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Counting ions in the expanded figure.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip counting ions in the figure and skip naming lattice types.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 16 shows that NaCl's attraction is not weak.
6_data_booklet.why: A lattice enthalpy of 790 kJ mol⁻¹ is a large energy, so the printed value contradicts any claim of weak forces.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking for the neighbour count; it is not in the booklet.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Alkali metal halide table: Na row, Cl column reads 790 kJ mol⁻¹.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NaCl's lattice arrangement and six neighbours per ion are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Three statements each break one fact of the model.
7_elimination.why: Ions held by electrostatic attraction exclude covalent bonds and weak forces, and known coordination excludes four.
7_elimination.avoid: Accepting A because polyatomic ions have covalent bonds; Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are single-atom ions.

definitely_wrong.rule: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are held by electrostatic attraction, not covalent bonds.
Ionic attractions are strong: section 16 gives 790 kJ mol⁻¹.
Each sodium ion in NaCl has six chloride neighbours, not four.

walkthrough.answer: D. Dissolving separates the ions. The others fail: the force is electrostatic attraction, it is strong, and each Na⁺ has six Cl⁻ neighbours.

cards.title: Ionic formula: know the polyatomic ion, then balance charges
cards.difficulty_signal: May 2025: over 70% correct and listed as well prepared (25M.1A.HL.6219.6). Older papers show recurring gaps with polyatomic ions (15M.3.HL.TZ1.17, 13N.2.SL.TZ0.3, 13M.2.SL.TZ2.5).

evidence.note: Answer D: Al₂(SO₄)₃.
Over 70% remembered the ion charges and deduced the formula.
Many HL candidates did not know the phosphate formula and charge; some gave phosphite or phosphide.
A large number could not write the correct charge or formula of nitrate.
Ammonium phosphate formula was often invented, including wrong phosphate formulas.
Many instances of NaO written for sodium oxide.
Few could deduce the charge on indium and the formula of indium sulfate.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.2: deduce formula and name of an ionic compound, including NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books drill swapping charges. Exams hide the difficulty in recalling the polyatomic ion exactly, with close-looking distractors.

trigger_phrases: total positive charge equals total negative charge
brackets around a multiplied polyatomic ion
trap_boundaries: Wrong phosphate formula or charge was reported as a basic failure (15M.3.HL.TZ1.17).
Using an element's ion such as phosphide in place of the polyatomic ion is a reported error (15M.3.HL.TZ1.17).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: A partial attempt gets the ratio but the wrong ion. Full credit needs both the exact ion and the balanced ratio.

disguises: Roman numeral in sulfate(VI)
Unfamiliar metal, such as indium or thallium, with its charge deduced
Formula embedded in a moles or equation question
3_novel_application.heuristic: Write each ion with its charge first; only then build the formula.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing, in both the MCQ and the short written form.

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip naming oxidation states of the atoms inside the polyatomic ion.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 10 prints each ionic radius with its charge, such as O 140 (2−). Polyatomic ions are NOT in the booklet and must be memorised.

rules: Wrong polyatomic ion rules out every option using it.
A 1:1 ratio needs equal and opposite charges; otherwise rule it out.

walkthrough.question:
Aluminium ions combine with sulfate(VI) ions. Which formula is correct for the compound formed?
A. AlSO₃
B. Al₂(SO₃)₃
C. AlSO₄
D. Al₂(SO₄)₃
walkthrough.key_idea: Al³⁺ and SO₄²⁻ balance only in a 2:3 ratio.
walkthrough.careful: Polyatomic formula and charge must be memorised exactly.
procedure: Write each ion with its charge.
Find the lowest ratio that makes total charge zero.
Bracket a polyatomic ion if more than one is needed.
Check that total positive equals total negative.
tricks: Swap charge numbers into subscripts; cancel if both subscripts share a factor.
Sulfate is SO₄²⁻, so any option with SO₃ falls at once.
if_lost: What charge does an aluminium ion carry?
What is the formula and charge of the sulfate ion?
What ratio of these ions makes the total charge zero?

1_context.short: Tests a formula built from a polyatomic ion.
1_context.why: The syllabus requires polyatomic ions by name and formula, so recalling sulfate correctly is the real test.
1_context.avoid: Reasoning from the VI in the name to a charge of 6−.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.2: deduce the formula of an ionic compound from its ions, including polyatomic ions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books practise charge swapping on given ions. Here you recall both ions, including a sulfate name with a Roman numeral.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The mark needs both the right ion and the 2:3 ratio.
2_markscheme_logic.why: Two Al³⁺ give 6+ and three SO₄²⁻ give 6−, so that is the lowest balanced ratio.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Forgetting ion charges; those who remembered them got this right (25M.1A.HL.6219.6).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: The right ratio with the SO₃ ion is still wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: B has the right ratio but the wrong ion. C has the right ion but the wrong ratio.

3_novel_application.short: The (VI) is the oxidation state of S, not the charge.
3_novel_application.why: Sulfur is +6 inside the ion, while the whole ion carries 2−, so the name adds no new step.
3_novel_application.avoid: Using the numeral as the ion's charge.
3_novel_application.disguise: Sulfate(VI) looks unfamiliar, but it is simply the ordinary sulfate ion.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ignore the numeral and write the ion you already memorised.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: one mark, with no credit for working.
4_command_terms.why: Each distractor pairs one correct idea with one error, so you need both parts right to pick out the answer.
4_command_terms.avoid: Selecting an option because one part looks right.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the formula with the correct ion and balanced charges.

5_time_efficiency.short: Write both ions, then balance: under twenty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: Writing the ions down first means two quick facts remove every wrong option.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Checking each option's total charge before knowing the ions.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip atom-by-atom oxidation states inside sulfate.

6_data_booklet.short: Polyatomic ions are not in the booklet; memorise them.
6_data_booklet.why: Section 10 shows charges for single-atom ions, but no table lists sulfate, so recall is unavoidable here.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 10 prints ionic charges beside radii, such as B 27 (3+) at the top of aluminium's group.
6_data_booklet.memorise: NH₄⁺, OH⁻, NO₃⁻, HCO₃⁻, CO₃²⁻, SO₄²⁻, PO₄³⁻ are NOT in the booklet.

7_elimination.short: Sulfate facts and 1:1 balance remove three options.
7_elimination.why: Two options use the wrong anion formula, and a 1:1 ratio cannot balance charges of 3+ and 2−.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping B because its ratio looks right.

definitely_wrong.rule: Uses SO₃ rather than SO₄, and 1:1 cannot balance 3+ and 2−.
Balanced ratio, but SO₃ is not the sulfate ion.
Correct anion, but 1:1 leaves 3+ against only 2−.

walkthrough.answer: D. Al₂(SO₄)₃: two Al³⁺ give 6+ and three SO₄²⁻ give 6−.

cards.title: Species in a compound: ions, not atoms, in formula and configuration
cards.difficulty_signal: Examiners report answers giving the atom instead of the ion, and removing 3d electrons rather than 4s (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6). No pct-correct figure is available for the 2025 question.

evidence.note: Answer D: Ca₃N₂ with Ca²⁺ as [Ar] and N³⁻ as [Ne].
A significant number gave the atom's formula, or lost electrons from 3d rather than 4s.
Configuration of S²⁻ given as 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, a full-shell ion.
Few deduced the charge on the indium ion and the formula of indium sulfate.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.1: predict the charge of an ion from the electron configuration of the atom, including transition elements with different charges.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books treat configuration and formula in separate chapters. Exams pair them in a single table row.

trigger_phrases: noble gas configuration after electron transfer
trap_boundaries: Giving the atom when the ion is asked for is a reported error (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6).
Transition ions lose 4s electrons before 3d; removing 3d first is a reported error (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Partial thinking gets the formula or the configurations. The full answer has both, since one row carries them together.

disguises: Word 'species' instead of ion
Nitride instead of a common halide
Transition metal ion such as Ni²⁺ where the 4s rule applies
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask what the atom becomes in the compound, then describe that.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: MCQ: one mark, all or nothing. Written ion configurations are a single point marked as correct or not (21M.2.SL.TZ1.1).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip full 1s notation when options use noble gas cores.

6_data_booklet.hack: Section 10 prints charges beside ionic radii, such as N 146 (3−). Electron configurations are NOT listed in the section text provided and must be built.

rules: A configuration matching the neutral atom is wrong for an ionic compound.
Group 1, 2 and 13 metals and Groups 15 to 17 non-metals reach noble gas cores; transition metals often do not.

walkthrough.question:
Calcium nitride contains one calcium species and one nitrogen species. Which row correctly gives the compound's formula and the electron configuration of each species?
A. Ca₂N₃; Ca species [Ar]; N species [Ne]
B. Ca₂N₃; Ca species [Ar] 4s²; N species [He] 2s² 2p³
C. Ca₃N₂; Ca species [Ar] 4s²; N species [He] 2s² 2p³
D. Ca₃N₂; Ca species [Ar]; N species [Ne]
walkthrough.key_idea: The compound holds Ca²⁺ and N³⁻, each with a noble gas core.
walkthrough.question_type: Ion charge, configuration and ionic formula
walkthrough.careful: Give the ion's configuration, not the atom's.
procedure: Find each element's valence electrons.
Decide electrons lost or gained to reach a noble gas.
Write each ion's configuration after that change.
Balance the ion charges to get the formula.
tricks: Configurations ending 4s² or 2p³ describe neutral atoms, so they cannot fit main-group ions.
Main-group only: transition metal ions lose 4s first and keep d electrons.
if_lost: Is this compound made of atoms or ions?
How many electrons does calcium lose, and nitrogen gain?
Which noble gas does each ion match?
What ratio of these ions cancels the charges?

1_context.short: Links the ion's charge, configuration and formula in one row.
1_context.why: The charge comes from the configuration, and the formula comes from the charge, so all three facts must agree.
1_context.avoid: Answering formula and configuration as separate facts.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.1: predict the charge of an ion from the electron configuration of the atom.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books teach ion formation and configuration separately. This row requires both for an unusual anion.

2_markscheme_logic.short: The right row needs correct formula and correct ion configurations.
2_markscheme_logic.why: An atom's configuration cannot describe what is in a compound, so both parts of the row must refer to ions.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Giving atoms instead of ions, as examiners reported for nickel (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6).
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: A correct formula with atoms' configurations is still wrong.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: C has the right formula but atoms' configurations. A has the right configurations but an unbalanced formula.

3_novel_application.short: 'Species' hides that the question means ions.
3_novel_application.why: Nitride is less familiar than chloride, but the same rule applies: gain electrons up to the next noble gas.
3_novel_application.avoid: Reading 'species' as atoms and copying the ground-state atoms.
3_novel_application.disguise: The neutral word 'species' and a less common anion make atom configurations look reasonable.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Replace 'species' with 'ion', then write the ion's charge.

4_command_terms.short: MCQ stem: a whole row must be correct for the mark.
4_command_terms.why: Rows mix one right part with one wrong part, so checking just one column cannot separate them.
4_command_terms.avoid: Stopping after checking only the formula column.
4_command_terms.demands: Choose the row where formula and both configurations are correct.

5_time_efficiency.short: Check one configuration, then the formula; two checks finish it.
5_time_efficiency.why: Two options repeat each wrong part, so one configuration and one formula are enough to isolate the row.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Writing out full 1s notation; options use cores.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip full subshell notation; the options use cores.

6_data_booklet.short: Section 10 gives nitrogen's ion charge directly.
6_data_booklet.why: The printed charge saves working it out, and it confirms a gain of three electrons to reach neon's configuration.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Reading N's atomic radius value instead of its ionic entry.
6_data_booklet.pattern: Section 10 shows N 146 (3−) and O 140 (2−) beside the atomic radii.
6_data_booklet.memorise: Electron configurations are NOT listed in the section text provided, so build them from valence electrons.

7_elimination.short: Unbalanced formulas and atom configurations remove three rows.
7_elimination.why: Charges must cancel in a neutral compound, and an ionic compound cannot contain neutral-atom configurations here.
7_elimination.avoid: Keeping C because its formula is right.

definitely_wrong.rule: Ca₂N₃ gives 4+ against 9−, so charges do not cancel.
Unbalanced formula, and its configurations are those of atoms.
[Ar] 4s² and [He] 2s² 2p³ are neutral atoms, not ions.

walkthrough.answer: D. Ca₃N₂: Ca²⁺ is [Ar] and N³⁻ is [Ne]; three 2+ balance two 3−.

cards.title: Sign first or number first: oxidation state versus ion charge
cards.difficulty_signal: Notation is an easy mark to lose: bare 2 and 2+ were refused in May 2025 (25M.2.HL.6209.6), and +3 for a charge was a common error (16N.3.HL.TZ0.4).

evidence.note: Oxidation state of S is +2 or II; bare 2 and 2+ are not accepted.
Change of −2 to +4 credited; the number-first form 2− to 4+ is not accepted.
Common error: writing +3, which is oxidation state notation, for a charge of 3+.
Most could deduce the oxidation number in a complex ion using the correct notation.

1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.1: ion charge from configuration, with transition elements forming ions of different charges. S2.1.2: polyatomic ions.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use both notations without comment. Exams refuse the wrong one even when the number is right.

trigger_phrases: +2 or II for an oxidation state
trap_boundaries: Bare 2 and 2+ are refused for an oxidation state (25M.2.HL.6209.6).
Number-first forms such as 2− to 4+ are refused for oxidation state changes (21M.2.SL.TZ1.1).
Writing +3 for a charge is reported as a common error (16N.3.HL.TZ0.4).
2_markscheme_logic.delta: The same value can earn zero or full marks: only the notation matching what was asked scores.

disguises: Oxidation state of an atom inside a ligand in a complex
Charge on an unfamiliar metal such as indium
Oxidation state change reported across a reaction
3_novel_application.heuristic: Ask whether the question means one atom's state or a whole ion's charge.

4_command_terms.score_mechanics: Usually one mark, all or nothing; value and notation must both be right (25M.2.HL.6209.6).

5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip the metal and neutral ligands; they do not affect atoms inside another ion.

6_data_booklet.hack: No table helps here. Oxidation state rules and notation are NOT in the section text provided and must be memorised.

rules: Number-first answers for an oxidation state are wrong by notation alone.
Sign-first answers for an ion charge are wrong by notation alone.

walkthrough.question:
Iron(III) ions react with thiosulfate ions. The first step forms a dark violet complex:
[Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺(aq) + 2S₂O₃²⁻(aq) → [Fe(S₂O₃)₂(H₂O)₂]⁻(aq) + 4H₂O(l)
Deduce the oxidation state of sulfur in the complex. [1]
walkthrough.key_idea: Thiosulfate's atoms sum to 2−, so S is +2; write sign first.
walkthrough.question_type: Deduce oxidation state and write its notation
walkthrough.careful: Sign goes before the number: +2, never 2+.
procedure: Find the ion that contains the atom.
Assign known states, with O as −2.
Set the sum of states equal to the ion's charge.
Solve for the unknown, then write the sign first.
tricks: Ignore iron and water: thiosulfate's own charge is given in the equation.
With two S atoms, the result is an average; it fails for individual atoms.
if_lost: Which ion in the formula contains the sulfur?
What is the overall charge of that ion?
What is the oxidation state of each oxygen?
How should an oxidation state be written, compared with a charge?

1_context.short: Tests working inside a polyatomic ion, and correct notation.
1_context.why: Ion charge and oxidation state use similar symbols but mean different things, so examiners test the distinction with one mark.
1_context.avoid: Writing it the way you would write an ion's charge.
1_context.syllabus_hook: S2.1.2: polyatomic ions; here the charge on thiosulfate is given in the equation.
1_context.textbook_gap: Books use simple binary examples. Here the atom sits in a ligand inside a transition metal complex.

2_markscheme_logic.short: Only +2 or II scores; 2 and 2+ score nothing.
2_markscheme_logic.why: The sign-first form names an oxidation state, while number-first names an ion's charge, so the notation carries meaning.
2_markscheme_logic.avoid: Number-first answers, refused here and in 21M.2.SL.TZ1.1.
2_markscheme_logic.trap_boundary: Bare 2 and 2+ are refused, even though the value is right.
2_markscheme_logic.delta: Correct arithmetic with 2+ scores zero. Writing +2 scores the mark.

3_novel_application.short: A big complex hides a simple calculation on one ion.
3_novel_application.why: The S atoms sit wholly within S₂O₃²⁻, so iron and water do not enter the sum.
3_novel_application.avoid: Including iron or water in the sum, which adds unknowns.
3_novel_application.disguise: A complex with brackets and a catalysed reaction context looks far harder than it is.
3_novel_application.heuristic: Circle the ion containing the atom, then ignore everything else.

4_command_terms.short: Deduce: use the given formula to reach one value.
4_command_terms.why: The equation supplies thiosulfate's charge, and one mark means only the final answer is checked.
4_command_terms.avoid: Explaining the complex's colour or structure here.
4_command_terms.demands: Reach sulfur's oxidation state from the charge shown on thiosulfate.
4_command_terms.score_mechanics: One mark, all or nothing; value and notation together.

5_time_efficiency.short: One equation, one answer: about thirty seconds.
5_time_efficiency.why: A single equation in one unknown is enough, so the rest of the long question stem can be ignored.
5_time_efficiency.avoid: Reading the whole reaction context before starting.
5_time_efficiency.fat_to_trim: Skip iron's state and the water ligands.

6_data_booklet.short: No booklet section helps here; rely on memorised rules.
6_data_booklet.why: The only data needed is the charge printed in the equation, so the booklet adds nothing to this step.
6_data_booklet.avoid: Looking up electronegativity in section 9 to assign states.
6_data_booklet.pattern: None: the equation gives thiosulfate's charge directly.
6_data_booklet.memorise: O is −2 in most compounds; the sign goes first. Neither is in the section text provided.

7_elimination.short: Rule out number-first answers and any negative value.
7_elimination.why: Notation decides the first case, and three O atoms at −2 force S positive for a total of 2−.

definitely_wrong.rule: Refused as oxidation state notation, whatever the value.
Three O give −6, so S must be positive to total −2.
Iron is outside the thiosulfate ion, so it does not enter.

walkthrough.answer: +2 (or II). In S₂O₃²⁻: 2x + 3(−2) = −2, so x = +2. Bare 2 or 2+ is not accepted.

cross_links.note: Periodic trends: ionic radius ordering and isoelectronic comparisons (18N.2.SL.TZ0.4, 24M.1.SL.TZ2.7), plus oxidation states from card S2.1-07.
Electron configurations of ions, including 4s before 3d removal for transition metals (24M.2.SL.TZ1.6).
Mole calculations behind moles of ions from a formula (24N.1.HL.TZ0.1).
Covalent bonding inside polyatomic ions such as ammonium (10M.1.SL.TZ1.9).
Lattice enthalpy values in section 16 come from Born–Haber cycles.
